explain.say: Look at your T-shirt. It is probably cotton, made in a factory. But before the 1760s, almost all cloth was spun and woven by hand at home. Then, in Britain, machines changed everything. The timeline shows how the factory age began.

faq.q: What did the spinning jenny do?
faq.a: Invented by James Hargreaves around 1764, it let one worker spin several threads at once, eight at first and later many more, by turning a single wheel.
Richard Arkwright's Cromford Mill in Derbyshire, built in 1771, is often called the first modern factory. It used water power and ran long shifts. Today it is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faq.q: How did steam engines change factories?
faq.a: Early mills needed rivers for water power. James Watt's improved steam engines, from the 1770s and 1780s, let factories be built in towns and cities, near coal and workers.

Yes. Many children worked long hours in mills, some as young as five or six, mending threads and cleaning under moving machines. The Factory Act of 1833 banned children under nine from textile mills and limited hours for older children.

faq.q: Was factory work better than home work?
faq.a: It depended. Factories paid regular wages and made cheap goods, but hours were long, rules were strict and machines were dangerous. Historians still debate whether living standards rose or fell at first.
